name: Agouti-related peptide
lead: Agouti-related peptide (AgRP) is a hypothalamic neuropeptide that raises appetite and lowers energy use by blocking melanocortin signalling. It is the natural counterpart to the melanocortin peptides (such as alpha-MSH) that suppress hunger, and it is relevant to physique goals because it is one of the brain's main hunger switches, central to how body fat is regulated [1][2].

AgRP is made in neurons of the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus, which co-release neuropeptide Y; these neurons are switched on by fasting and by ghrelin and are restrained by leptin and insulin [3][4][5]. AgRP was identified in 1997 as an antagonist of the melanocortin 3 and 4 receptors [6][18].

Research on AgRP is laboratory and clinical-physiology work rather than a consumer product. A registered phase 2 trial listed a safety study of AgRP inhibition for obesity and weight loss (n=100) [7], and other registered studies examine AgRP levels alongside growth hormone treatment [8]. Because it is an endogenous signal, people in appearance communities mostly discuss it in terms of hunger control and leanness.

For readers interested in body composition, AgRP matters because hunger drive is the main practical obstacle to getting leaner: AgRP neurons are the cells that turn hunger on during fasting and dieting, and many appetite-related drugs and hormones act on the circuit they control.[2][4]

chain: AgRP neurons drive hunger when energy is low
Blocking melanocortin receptors reduces satiety signalling
Hunger and energy expenditure set body-fat level
angle.text: AgRP is the brain's hunger signal; understanding it explains why appetite rises during dieting and why drugs targeting the melanocortin pathway are studied for weight control. It is a biological target rather than something people take.

paras: AgRP neurons increase food intake and reduce energy expenditure when the body is in negative energy balance [2][5]. Experiments in mice show that rapid activation of these neurons is sufficient to start feeding, and that they are needed for feeding in adults [9][10]. AgRP blocks MC3R and MC4R, the receptors through which POMC-derived peptides signal fullness [6][1].

Ghrelin, the stomach hunger hormone, acts on these neurons [11]. Leptin acting on inhibitory neurons dampens their tone toward POMC neurons [12]. AgRP neurons also help control other processes, including liver autophagy during energy deprivation [13] and reproductive hormone axes in obesity [14].
Reviews describe AgRP/NPY and POMC neurons as potential obesity treatment targets [5]. A small pilot study examined how prolonged exercise affects circulating AgRP [15].

The AGRP gene sits on human chromosome 16q22 and encodes a 132-residue precursor that is processed into a mature peptide of roughly 112 amino acids, whose folded C-terminal domain is a compact cystine knot that is stable to heat and acid.[19][18] The protein is about 25 percent identical to agouti signalling protein (ASIP), the molecule that controls coat colour in mammals, which is where its name comes from.[19]

Two independent teams identified AgRP in 1997, using its sequence similarity to ASIP.[19][6] Early experiments showed that mice made to overexpress AgRP became heavy and hyperphagic, resembling the obese lethal-yellow agouti mouse in which ASIP is ectopically expressed, but without a change in coat colour; this helped establish AgRP as a natural antagonist of the brain's melanocortin receptors.[18][19]

AgRP acts as a competitive antagonist and inverse agonist at the melanocortin 3 and 4 receptors (MC3R and MC4R), blocking the fullness signal that alpha-MSH from neighbouring POMC neurons delivers.[19][6] Because it is selective for those two receptors, its action is essentially a brake on the melanocortin satiety pathway.[19]

AgRP neurons also release neuropeptide Y and the inhibitory transmitter GABA, which give a fast onset to hunger while AgRP itself works over hours.[18][17] Ghrelin from the stomach stimulates them, leptin restrains them, and their activity rises during fasting.[11][12][19] In mice, switching these neurons on rapidly triggers feeding without training, and a 2005 study found that adult mice lose the ability to feed when the neurons are ablated.[9][10]

In human genetics, inherited mutations in leptin, the leptin receptor, POMC and MC4R cause severe obesity, and reviews cite the AgRP-POMC circuit as the framework for understanding these syndromes.[20] Polymorphisms in the AGRP gene have been linked in some studies to obesity and to anorexia nervosa.[19]

Because AgRP neurons are the hunger-promoting arm of energy balance, discussions of fat loss and cutting often refer to them indirectly: the hunger that rises during a calorie deficit is partly an AgRP-neuron effect.[2][4] Researchers have also looked at how exercise changes circulating appetite peptides, including AgRP, NPY and alpha-MSH. A 2012 pilot study assessed prolonged exercise,[15] and a 2024 crossover trial in twelve adults examined whether greater lactate accumulation, induced with sodium bicarbonate, altered peripheral NPY, AgRP and alpha-MSH concentrations.[21]

Recent circuit work suggests that GLP-1 signalling, the pathway targeted by drugs such as semaglutide, interacts with hunger-sensing hypothalamic circuits, and a 2024 Nature Metabolism study mapped a GLP-1-sensitive satiety circuit.[22] A 2025 Cell Metabolism paper reported acute and circadian feedforward regulation of AgRP neurons.[23]

sections.h: History: from yellow mice to a hunger peptide
paras: The name comes from the agouti mouse, whose banded wild-type coat is produced by a signalling protein that switches hair follicle melanocytes from black-brown eumelanin to yellow pheomelanin. Mouse geneticists studied the agouti locus from the 1950s, and a molecular characterisation of the gene followed in 1992.[26] Dominant mutations such as lethal yellow cause the agouti protein to be made throughout the body, producing a yellow coat together with obesity and insulin resistance, which is how the same locus came to be linked with body weight.[26]

In 1994 researchers showed that agouti protein antagonises the receptor for melanocyte-stimulating hormone, and in 1995 ectopic agouti expression in transgenic mice was tied to obesity and diabetes-like features.[26] In 1997 a related gene, found with raised hypothalamic expression in obese and diabetic mice, was described and later became known as agouti-related protein or peptide (AgRP); it blocks the same melanocortin receptors in the brain rather than in the skin.[26][6] Structural work showed that these proteins share a compact cystine-knot fold.[26][19]

Agouti-signaling protein (ASIP), the skin-pigment relative, and AgRP, the brain relative, are distinct genes with overlapping pharmacology: both antagonise melanocortin receptors. ASIP acts on MC1R in follicular melanocytes to favour lighter pheomelanin, while AgRP acts mainly on MC3R and MC4R in the hypothalamus to promote feeding.[26][19] The human ASIP gene is expressed more broadly than its mouse counterpart, including in fat tissue, and is thought to influence hair-colour quality in people.[26]

This shared family is the reason AgRP appears in discussions of the melanocortin system alongside peptides sold in appearance communities for tanning or appetite effects. AgRP itself is a research neuropeptide and has no consumer or prescription product.

sections.h: Relevance to leanness and body composition
paras: Fat loss involves fighting hunger, and AgRP neurons are the brain cells that translate a calorie deficit, low leptin and high ghrelin into appetite.[2][4][11][12] Rodent work shows that activating them is enough to start feeding and that they are suppressed by leptin and by gut and incretin signals.[9][12] A 2024 connectomics study described a circuit in which GLP-1 signalling dampens appetite-related neural pathways, which researchers frame as part of how GLP-1 drugs reduce hunger.[22]

For readers interested in staying lean, this gives a mechanistic picture of why hunger rises during a cut and why appetite-regulating medicines work on this pathway. A small pilot study in people examined how prolonged exercise changes circulating AgRP, and a later study looked at lactate and peripheral hormone concentrations.[15][21]

Registered trials include a phase 2 safety study of AgRP inhibition for obesity (NCT00779519) [7], growth hormone and liraglutide effects on AgRP in healthy adults [8], and AgRP in preeclampsia [16]. No consumer AgRP product is described in the literature.

Human work on AgRP is mostly physiological. A 2024 randomized crossover trial of twelve adults measured peripheral appetite peptides after exercise with or without sodium bicarbonate.[21] A 2016 study reported changes in the melanocortin pathway in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis,[24] and registered studies measure AgRP alongside growth hormone and liraglutide treatment in healthy adults and in children with growth hormone deficiency.[8][25]

card.summary: The brain's own hunger-driving peptide that blocks satiety receptors; studied as a lever for appetite and body-fat control.

quick.overview:
AgRP is a peptide made by hunger-sensing neurons in the hypothalamus. When energy runs low, these neurons fire and push appetite up while lowering energy use.

It matters for people working on leanness because it is one of the pathways that makes dieting feel hard, and researchers study it as a target for weight control.
quick.mechanism: AgRP blocks melanocortin 3 and 4 receptors, cancelling the fullness signal from POMC neurons. The same neurons release NPY and GABA for fast hunger drive.
quick.risks: AgRP is an endogenous signal rather than a drug, and no approved therapy targets it directly. Changing this pathway affects appetite, metabolism and growth/reproductive axes.
